q: A dog is presented with suspicion of sexual abuse and has a normal physical examination with no external injuries. Which statement best guides the next step?
o: Absence of injury does not exclude sexual abuse, so proceed with the full forensic protocol, including alternate light source examination, DNA swabs and cavity flush.
Absence of injury excludes sexual abuse, so no further workup is needed.
Bathe the animal first to allow a cleaner examination, then reassess.
e: Many animals show no visible injury, and bathing destroys biological evidence.

q: In a forensic examination for suspected sexual abuse, when should the rectal temperature be taken?
o: Last, after swabs, flush samples and physical examination are complete
First, as part of baseline vital signs
After the alternate light source examination but before swabs
e: The thermometer can contaminate the area or disturb evidence, so temperature comes last.

q: You collect DNA swabs from the vaginal orifice of a dog suspected of sexual abuse. What does the ASPCA protocol specify?
o: One swab per area, placed in a sealed plastic tube with transport medium
At least two swabs per area, air-dried, stored in paper envelopes with chain-of-custody labelling
Three swabs per area, frozen at −20°C (−4°F) in a sealed plastic container
e: Two swabs allow duplicate analysis, and air-drying in paper preserves DNA.

q: A vaginal cavity flush is collected as a forensic sample. Which container and temperature are appropriate?
o: A purple-top EDTA tube, frozen at −20°C (−4°F)
A red-top tube with no additives, refrigerated at 4°C (39.2°F)
A container of 10% buffered formalin at room temperature
e: Flush fluid is collected in a sterile plain tube and refrigerated to preserve sperm and DNA.

q: Which finding is most consistent with penetration injury, rather than restraint injury, in a suspected sexual abuse case?
o: Ligature marks around the muzzle
Bilateral flank bruising from gripping
Bruising and lacerations of the vulvar lips with reduced vaginal tone
e: Restraint injuries appear on the head, neck and flanks. Penetration injuries affect the genital and rectal tissues.

q: Spermatozoa are found in the urine sediment of a female dog. Why is this significant?
o: It is a normal finding in intact bitches in oestrus.
It shows the dog was bred without owner consent, which is not a cruelty concern.
Sperm can reach the bladder through the short female urethra after vaginal assault, a specific finding supporting sexual abuse.
e: Spermatozoa in the urine of a female dog are abnormal and forensically significant.

q: Why does the ASPCA protocol recommend a follow-up examination at 24 to 48 hours?
o: DNA evidence degrades after 24 hours and must be collected again.
Bruising and mucosal tears may not be visible at first and can evolve over the following 24 to 48 hours.
A second examiner must verify all findings for legal purposes.
e: Soft tissue injuries from penetration can develop over the first two days.

q: Which forensic light source setting does the ASPCA sexual abuse protocol specify for a surface examination?
o: A 415 nm excitation light with orange-tinted goggles, or a Wood's lamp with appropriate filters
Standard white light with a magnifying glass
Infrared light at 900 nm with a clear filter
e: Forensic light sources at about 415 nm make body fluids fluoresce, and orange goggles filter the background.
